title: Accessibility as a foundation for usable interaction
outcome: Check semantics, names, focus, contrast, motion, and zoom as part of the main flow.
useCase: Every reusable component and critical business flow.
benefits: Improves access and often clarifies interaction for everyone.
drawbacks: Custom widgets carry ongoing keyboard and semantics responsibilities.
version: Web UX · WCAG 2.2 · principles, not magic formulas
cue: Name it. Reach it. Operate it. Understand it.

trace.title: Semantic structure
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

Accessibility is not a final color check. A person must be able to perceive the state, operate controls, understand the result, and use compatible assistive technology.

Native HTML gives many behaviors that a clickable div does not.

Every interactive control needs an understandable name. Focus must be visible and move predictably.

A modal needs a labelled dialog context, a deliberate focus path, and a way to close it. Errors and async status should be announced appropriately without narrating every keystroke.

Use WCAG 2.2 success criteria as requirements to check, with their exact scope and exceptions.

Automated tools catch some issues; they cannot tell whether the action name makes sense or whether a real task is understandable. Combine automated checks, keyboard use, zoom, and assistive-technology testing.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Complete the same task without a mouse. Can you reach every control, see focus, understand its name, operate it, and recover from failure?

Then zoom the page and inspect reflow. Then test the key path with a screen reader.

Respect reduced-motion preferences for unnecessary animation. Avoid information conveyed only by color, hover, or movement.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: Adding role=button to a div without keyboard behavior creates a misleading contract. A focus trap that cannot be escaped is a defect. aria-hidden content can still contain focusable elements if implemented carelessly.
